function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to walk you through what you’d need to do, but I don’t have the ability to actually run `git clone`, edit files on your machine, or push commits back to GitHub. Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can follow locally (or in a CI environment) to achieve the same result. I’ll also give you ready‑to‑paste templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow so you can copy them into the repository after you’ve cloned it.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# SSH URL – make sure you have the proper key set up
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you prefer HTTPS, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` and use your GitHub credentials.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Create Required Files

### 2.1 Inspect the Project Structure

Run:

```bash
tree -L 2
```

Typical output for a minimal Node.js project looks like this:

```
nodejs-welcome/
├── src/
│   └── index.js
├── package.json
└── README.md
```

* `src/index.js` – entry point of the application  
* `package.json` – contains dependencies and start script

If the structure differs, adjust the paths in the templates below accordingly.

---

### 2.2 Create/Update the Dockerfile

**Template (`Dockerfile`)**

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Define the command to run the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and suitable for most Node apps.  
> * `npm ci` ensures reproducible installs from `package-lock.json`.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the typical Express default; change if your app uses another port.

Place this file at the root of the repository (`nodejs-welcome/Dockerfile`). If a Dockerfile already exists, review it and merge the changes above.

---

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes Deployment & Service

**Deployment (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)**

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

**Service (`k8s/service.yaml`)**

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to ClusterIP/NodePort if needed
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Folder structure**  
> Create a folder called `k8s/` at the root of the repo and place both YAML files there.

> **Image name**  
> Replace `<YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image name you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`).

---

### 2.4 Add a GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
        cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache

    - name: Clean up cache
      run: rm -rf /tmp/.buildx-cache
```

> **What this does**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the Docker image using Buildx (supports caching).  
> * Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry under the same name as the repo.  

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Ensure the repository has the `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret (it’s automatically available).  
> * If you’re using a different registry, update the login and tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage All New/Updated Files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you added the `k8s/` folder, you may want to add it recursively:

```bash
git add k8s/
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, building and publishing the Docker image.

---

## Quick Checklist

| Step | Command | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| Clone | `git clone ...` | |
| Inspect | `tree -L 2` | |
| Create Dockerfile | `nano Dockerfile` | Paste template |
| Create K8s folder | `mkdir k8s && nano k8s/deployment.yaml` | |
| Create Service | `nano k8s/service.yaml` | |
| Create Actions workflow | `mkdir -p .github/workflows && nano .github/workflows/docker-build.yml` | |
| Stage | `git add ...` | |
| Commit | `git commit -m "...` | |
| Push | `git push origin main` | |

---

### What Next?

Once the image is built and pushed, you can deploy it to a cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

Make sure you have `kubectl` configured to talk to your cluster and that the image registry is accessible from the cluster nodes.

---

Let me know if you hit any snags while setting this up!
